displayQuote: Art is what you can get away with

meta.title: Who really said "Art is what you can get away with"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Andy Warhol. The documented line is Marshall McLuhan's — "Art is anything you can get away with," in The Medium is the Massage (1967).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Art is what you can get away with'?
meta.ogDescription: Warhol gets the credit; McLuhan wrote it. The 1967 book, the real wording, and how the misattribution spread — sourced and checkable.

answer.label: Not Andy Warhol — actually Marshall McLuhan
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented appearance is in The Medium is the Massage (Bantam Books, 1967), the picture-book McLuhan made with designer Quentin Fiore, where the line runs in display type across pages 132–136 — and the documented wording is “Art is anything you can get away with.” Quote Investigator, which verified the book in hardcopy, credits McLuhan and records no Warhol attestation anywhere in its chronology; the familiar “what” version circulates under Warhol’s name with no source attached.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: The Medium is the Massage: An Inventory of Effects
Marshall McLuhan & Quentin Fiore; produced by Jerome Agel
Spread across pages 132–136 (verified with hardcopy by Quote Investigator)

source.excerpt:
Art is anything you can get away with.

[facing photographs, captioned] “The biggest and best woman in the world,” an 82-foot-long, 20-foot-high sculpture, in Moderna Museet, Stockholm. You can walk around in her.
trail: 1967 — earliest located appearance. Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest close match it found is in The Medium is the Massage by McLuhan and Fiore, spread over pages 132 to 136, verified with hardcopy of the Bantam Books edition.

February and April 1967 — it escapes the book. Quote Investigator cites a February 25, 1967 Camden, New Jersey Courier-Post item quoting it from the forthcoming book, and an April 13, 1967 Daily Tar Heel report of it chalked on the ground at a Chapel Hill “chalk-in” — full chronology ↗.

1968 — credited to McLuhan in print. Alan Levy’s The Culture Vultures uses the line with an explicit credit: “McLuhan has also said, ‘Art is anything you can get away with’” — quoted by Quote Investigator ↗.

The Warhol version has no such trail. The “what you can get away with” wording circulates under Warhol’s name on unsourced aggregator pages — Goodreads ↗ gives no book, no date, and flags its quotes as community-added and unverified.
source.excerptNote: The book is a designed collage rather than continuous prose — the sentence is set in large type running across five pages, facing photographs of a colossal walk-in sculpture. Text as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from a hardcopy of the 1967 Bantam edition.

author.name: Marshall McLuhan
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Herbert Marshall McLuhan (July 21, 1911 – December 31, 1980) was a Canadian philosopher whose work is a cornerstone of media theory — the man behind The Gutenberg Galaxy (1962), Understanding Media (1964) and the coinages “the medium is the message” and “the global village.” He spent most of his career at the University of Toronto. The Medium is the Massage (1967), made with graphic designer Quentin Fiore and produced by Jerome Agel, was his bestseller: a collage of aphorisms set against photographs, which is exactly the form in which this line appears.

misattribution.heading: Where the Warhol credit comes from
misattribution.intro: This is a wording swap and a name swap at once. The version that travels under Andy Warhol’s name (“what you can get away with”) is not the version anyone has documented, and no primary Warhol source — book, interview, diary or film — has ever been produced for it.

items.why: Goodreads ↗ carries “Art is what you can get away with.” credited simply to “— Andy Warhol,” with 613 likes, no book, no date, and the site’s own note that quotes are community-added and unverified. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ of the saying names McLuhan, Fiore, Frank Richardson, Terence Trent D’Arby and Theodor W. Adorno — and does not mention Warhol at any point.

The print seller McGaw Graphics ↗ sells a poster whose title is the line itself, listed under Warhol as the artist, with an Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts copyright notice on the page. A quote on a wall in a frame is very hard to argue with.

Wikiquote ↗ lists “Art is anything you can get away with” under Understanding Media (1964), without a page number, and a “whatever” variant under the 1967 book. Writing to the American Dialect Society list, Garson O’Toole reported: “The Wikiquote webpage for McLuhan claims that this remark is in his book ‘Understanding Media’ (1964), but I accessed that book, and the quotation was absent” — ADS-L, August 2022 ↗.

items.scope: Other names it has picked up
items.who: Terence Trent D’Arby and Theodor W. Adorno
items.why: Per Quote Investigator ↗, a 2000 collection compiled by Vincent Fu printed the line credited to the singer Terence Trent D’Arby, and a 2006 book by Bhesham R. Sharma presented it as “in line with Adorno’s view” — though without directly crediting Adorno.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented sentence is McLuhan’s, it reads “Art is anything you can get away with,” and its earliest located home is The Medium is the Massage (1967) — Quote Investigator ↗, verified with hardcopy.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Warhol
lead: The line is a joke about the art market, and Warhol was the art market’s face — the man who sold soup cans as paintings. So the aphorism fits him better than it fits a Toronto English professor, which is most of the reason it drifted. But McLuhan and Warhol were working the same territory in the same years, and the traffic ran the other way: The Medium is the Massage came out in 1967, at the height of the Factory, and McLuhan was already the era’s designated explainer of media and celebrity.

The saying has kept doing real work. In 2022, ruling on the copyright suit over Maurizio Cattelan’s banana taped to a gallery wall, a U.S. district judge reached for it — and credited McLuhan, not Warhol: “a banana taped to a wall recalls Marshall McLuhan’s definition of art—‘anything you can get away with.’” That courtroom citation is what prompted Quote Investigator’s inquiry ↗ in the first place.
context.detailsSummary: What the page actually looks like
detailsBody: The Medium is the Massage is a designed object, not a book of paragraphs: Fiore laid McLuhan’s aphorisms across full-bleed spreads. That is why Quote Investigator cites the line as pages 132 to 136 rather than a single page — the sentence is broken up and set large across five pages.

The photographs facing it show a colossal walk-in sculpture, captioned in the book as “The biggest and best woman in the world,” an 82-foot-long, 20-foot-high sculpture in the Moderna Museet, Stockholm. In a 2022 American Dialect Society mailing-list post ↗, quote researcher Garson O’Toole identified the sculpture as Niki de Saint Phalle’s, noting a webpage giving its title as “She – a Cathedral.”

The phrase escaped into the wild fast. Quote Investigator records a Camden, New Jersey newspaper flagging it as a “pearl on art” from the forthcoming book on February 25, 1967, and student journalists at Chapel Hill reporting it chalked on the ground at a Fine Arts Festival “chalk-in” on April 13, 1967.
context.pull: The documented wording is “anything,” not “what” — and the name on it is McLuhan.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest close match Quote Investigator located appeared in the 1967 book The Medium is the Massage by Marshall McLuhan and Quentin Fiore, spread across pages 132-136 (Bantam Books, verified with hardcopy); QI concludes McLuhan deserves full credit. The article's chronology also covers a 1907 Frank Richardson analogue, a Feb 25 1967 Camden Courier-Post item, an April 13 1967 Daily Tar Heel chalk-in report, Alan Levy's 1968 credit to McLuhan, a 1992 Guardian Notes & Queries exchange, a 2000 credit to Terence Trent D'Arby, a 2006 link to Adorno, and the 2022 Cattelan banana ruling. Andy Warhol is not mentioned anywhere in the article.

Garson O'Toole wrote to the American Dialect Society list: 'The Wikiquote webpage for McLuhan claims that this remark is in his book "Understanding Media" (1964), but I accessed that book, and the quotation was absent,' and identified the 1967 Medium is the Massage as the earliest close match; he also identified the accompanying photograph as Niki de Saint Phalle's sculpture, titled per a linked webpage 'She - a Cathedral'. The thread does not mention Andy Warhol.

Wikiquote's Marshall McLuhan page lists 'Art is anything you can get away with.' under the Understanding Media (1964) section (without a page number, unlike neighbouring entries) and 'Art is whatever you can get away with.' under The Medium is the Massage (1967).
Wikiquote's Andy Warhol page does not contain the phrase 'get away with' anywhere.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of 'the medium is the massage an inventory of effects' by Marshall McLuhan, published by Bantam Books, Inc., 1967, 166 pages.
The Medium Is the Massage was co-created by Marshall McLuhan and graphic designer Quentin Fiore with coordination by Jerome Agel, and was published by Bantam Books in 1967.

Jeff Jacoby's September 2023 column states that Marshall McLuhan 'famously declared (in an aphorism often misattributed to Andy Warhol): Art is anything you can get away with', linking to Quote Investigator.
Goodreads displays 'Art is what you can get away with.' credited to '― Andy Warhol' with 613 likes, no book or source cited, and a note that quotes are community-added and not verified by Goodreads.

McGaw Graphics sells a poster/print titled 'Art is what you can get away with' attributed to Andy Warhol, with a copyright notice reading '©/®/™ 2026 The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc.'

Herbert Marshall McLuhan (July 21, 1911 – December 31, 1980) was a Canadian philosopher whose work is among the cornerstones of media theory; his books include The Gutenberg Galaxy (1962), Understanding Media (1964) and The Medium Is the Massage (1967), and he was primarily affiliated with the University of Toronto.
Andy Warhol (born Andrew Warhola Jr.; August 6, 1928 – February 22, 1987) was an American artist and filmmaker.
